analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from considering climate change or greenhouse gas emissions in environmental reviews of major projects.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the federal environmental review process under the National Environmental Policy Act. Agencies could not consider how a proposed project or its alternatives affect climate change or how greenhouse gas emissions affect climate, could not consider alternatives the project sponsor finds unworkable, and had to produce at most one of each review document per project. Sponsors could hire and pay a third party to write the official environmental review, which the agency could then adopt, and federal agencies could not reissue 2016 guidance on weighing emissions in reviews unless Congress authorized it. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never moved again. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Project sponsors — companies building highways, pipelines, mines, and other projects needing federal approval — would get faster, narrower reviews with fewer documents, no climate analysis, and review documents written by consultants they hired and paid. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: For any project needing an environmental impact statement, the agency would have to produce at most one impact statement, one environmental assessment, and one record of decision, cutting repeat or layered reviews. [S3]

Agencies would be barred from considering whether a proposed action or any alternative affects climate change, and from considering the effects of greenhouse gas emissions on climate, removing those issues from the review entirely. [S3]

A project sponsor could hire and pay a qualified third party to prepare the official environmental document, which the agency could adopt after reviewing it for compliance, instead of preparing the analysis itself. [S3]

Agencies would be required to reuse findings and research from prior NEPA reviews and could adopt documents prepared under state law, and categorical exclusions approved by other agencies or Congress could be used without further approval. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Communities living near federally approved projects would lose the part of the review that examines climate and emissions effects, and would face reviews whose alternatives and underlying analysis are shaped by the sponsor's own hired consultants; the public cost of project emissions would no longer be counted in federal decisions. [S3]

drawbacks.text: The bill's own text acknowledges that federal reviews impose real time and cost burdens by requiring annual reports tracking how long each type of review takes and its comprehensive cost — the strongest good-faith argument for streamlining is that slow reviews delay projects, including transit and other infrastructure. [S3]

However, the bill goes well beyond streamlining: it removes climate change and greenhouse gases from review altogether and restricts alternatives to those the sponsor deems technically and economically feasible, so the review would no longer weigh the full range of public costs. [S3]

Allowing the project sponsor to hire and pay the firm that writes the official environmental document — even with agency oversight and independence requirements — ties the reviewer's paycheck to the sponsor's success. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some of the bill's procedural provisions — a single lead agency for multi-agency projects, document limits, and reporting on review timelines — are the kind of streamlining that has bipartisan appeal. But its core would have deleted climate and emissions analysis from federal environmental review and let sponsors fund their own review documents, changes that benefit project sponsors directly and shift uncounted costs onto the public. The drawbacks are serious.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on September 16, 2020, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. [S5]
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities and others who rely on federal environmental reviews came out ahead: the existing process, including consideration of climate and emissions effects, remained in place. Project sponsors gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on September 16, 2020.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or floor action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote in either chamber, and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on it was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Project sponsors (pipelines, mines, highways, real estate development)
industries.note: The bill would have speeded approvals, capped review documents, barred agencies from weighing climate or emissions effects, and limited alternatives to those the sponsor deems feasible — all benefits flowing to whoever wants a federal approval, with the uncounted costs landing on the public. [S3]

Sponsors could hire and pay a qualified third party to write the official environmental document for agency adoption, creating a new revenue stream — though the firm's fee would come from the sponsor whose project it reviews. [S3]
